entries.title: missus
entries.definition:
A missus (from missus dominicus, "envoy of the lord") was a royal inspector Charlemagne and his heirs sent out to check that local counts and bishops were ruling fairly and collecting what the crown was owed. Think FBI / federal inspector general, not "Mrs."

If a missus turns up in the books or in gossip, someone important is looking at your neighborhood.

entries.title: Manses
entries.definition:
A mansus (plural often written manses in estate lists) was a peasant farmstead unit — house, garden, and the strips of land that fed one household. Rough modern sense: "households on the tax roll," not mansions.

When the books say how many manses you have, they're counting productive families, not bedrooms.

entries.title: modii / modius
entries.definition:
A modius (plural modii) is a dry measure for grain. The classical Roman modius was about 8.7 liters — roughly 2 US dry gallons, or a bit under a peck (a peck is 8 dry quarts). Picture a sturdy bucket of wheat, not a truckload.

Exact medieval sizes wandered by region, but in the game it's your grain "bushel-ish" unit on the ledger.

entries.title: denarii / denarius
entries.definition:
The denarius (plural denarii) is the silver penny of the Frankish world. Charlemagne's reform (c. 793–794) struck about 240 of them from a pound of silver (~1.7 g of silver each). Accounting still used the old trio: 12 denarii = 1 solidus (shilling of account), 20 solidi = 1 pound — the ancestor of Britain's £sd system.

In game terms: your cash. A handful of denarii is grocery money; hundreds are serious.

entries.title: demesne
entries.definition:
Demesne (say "di-MAIN") is the land the lord keeps for his own working — not rented out to free tenants. Modern hook: the company's owned factories vs franchisees; or a ranch's "home place" vs leased pastures.

Labour, seed, and harvest on the demesne hit your chest and stores directly.

entries.title: pagus
entries.definition:
A pagus was a rural district — bigger than a village, smaller than a whole kingdom. "Pagus of Autun" is like saying "Autun County."

It tells you whose orbit Fontenay sits in for law, markets, and trouble.

entries.title: cell of Saint-Martin
entries.definition: Fontenay's little monastic house under Saint Martin's patronage — a few brothers, a timber oratory, and a claim on local tithes and prayers, under a larger abbey's shadow.

entries.title: cell
entries.definition: Here cell means a small monastic house (Latin cella), not a prison cell. Tiny community of monks or nuns under a larger abbey's shadow — a religious "branch office" with a chapel, a few brothers, and claims on local tithes and prayers.

entries.title: pannage / mast
entries.definition:
Pannage is turning pigs into the woods in autumn to fatten on fallen nuts. Mast is that nut fall. A good mast year is a bumper crop of woodland calories.

Modern hook: free-range finishing on seasonal forage.

entries.title: bloomery
entries.definition:
A bloomery is a small charcoal furnace that turns ore into a spongy lump of iron called a bloom. Not a modern blast furnace.

Bloom iron is that rough product.

entries.title: mill leat
entries.definition:
A leat is a dug channel that leads river flow to a mill wheel.

Modern hook: millrace / dedicated water channel.

entries.title: two-field
entries.definition:
Half the arable sown, half fallow each year, then swap.

Early medieval soil rest before wider three-field use.

entries.title: villa
entries.definition:
Carolingian estate center (hall, stores, lands), not a vacation villa.

Fontenay is a working manor hub.

entries.title: overgrown waste
entries.definition:
Uncultivated marginal ground, not garbage.

In the land labels, waste is the tired edge of the holding that can be improved back to meadow or tillage.

entries.title: overgrown scrub
entries.definition:
Brush that can be cleared to arable.

In the land labels, scrub is overgrown cover waiting on labour and iron, not a cleaning verb.

entries.title: marling
entries.definition: Spreading chalky/clay-lime earth to improve soil; like liming a field.

entries.title: village reeve
entries.definition: Village headman / peasant go-between. On this estate that is Otto — he speaks for the hides and who is shirking.

entries.title: timber oratory
entries.definition: Small prayer house/chapel, not a speech. Timber means wooden — Fontenay's oratory is a modest timber chapel, not a stone church.

entries.title: feast days
entries.definition: Church holy days when ordinary field work stops.

entries.title: Francia
entries.definition: Frankish realm under the Carolingians; not the modern French Republic.

entries.title: Carolingian
entries.definition: Of Charlemagne's dynasty/era (late 700s–900s).

entries.title: Louis the Pious
entries.definition: Charlemagne's son; emperor in 825 (814–840).

entries.title: Alemannic
entries.definition: From Alemannia / later Swabia region.

entries.title: Lombard
entries.definition: From Lombardy / north Italian Lombard world.

entries.title: Frank / Frankish
entries.definition: Frankish people / identity in the Carolingian world.

entries.title: tithe
entries.definition: Church share (~tenth) of produce; a standing religious claim on the estate's grain and a little wool.

entries.title: renders
entries.definition: Obligations owed upward to a higher lord / public power; overlord taxes, not a cooking verb.

entries.title: standing order
entries.definition:
Ongoing written estate rule (not bank autopay).

Confirm is what writes one into the customs book; speech alone does not.

entries.title: lasting custom
entries.definition:
A rule or effect recorded as how the estate is run — a custom of the hall, lasting or for a time.

These sit in the customs book beside standing orders.

entries.title: hunt
entries.definition: Here a hunt is Gerulf taking a purse and walking the roads to find scarce goods — not a deer drive. He quotes a price and a span of seasons; the coin leaves the chest when you Confirm.

entries.title: hides
entries.definition:
Animal skins in the stores — leather-to-be — not the old English land-measure "hide," unless the sentence is clearly about land.

A few hides on the ledger are a tannery's raw stock, not a count of acres.

entries.title: muster
entries.definition: Call-up of men for local military or guard duty.

entries.title: prior
entries.definition:
Head of the small monastic house. At Fontenay that is Ermenald, prior of Saint-Martin's cell.

"Prior season" and "prior to" stay ordinary English.

entries.title: the hall
entries.definition: Seat of household authority — the timber hall at Fontenay — not a corridor.
